The cruise liner SS Morro Castle, burnt and grounded on the New Jersey coast. 1934

SS Morro Castle was an ocean liner built for voyages between New York City and Havana, Cuba. The ship was named for the Morro Castle fortress that guards the entrance to Havana Bay. Her success was in part due to Prohibition, as such trips provided a relatively affordable and (more importantly) legal means of enjoying a non-stop drinking party.

On the morning of September 8, 1934, en route from Havana to New York, the ship caught fire and burned, killing 137 passengers and crew members (out of a total of 549). The fire quickly burned through the ship's main electrical cables, plunging the ship into darkness and disabling the radio so that the crew were unable to issue a single SOS transmission. At about the same time, the wheelhouse lost the ability to steer the ship, as those hydraulic lines were severed by the fire as well. Only six of the ship's 12 lifeboats were launched and although the combined capacity of these boats was 408, they carried only 85 people, most of them crew members. Most passengers jumped from the deck and many died for lack of knowledge of how to use the life preservers.

The ship eventually beached herself near Asbury Park, New Jersey, and remained there for several months until she was towed off and scrapped.

The fire was a catalyst for improved shipboard fire safety. Today, the use of fire-retardant materials, automatic fire doors, ship-wide fire alarms, and greater attention to fire drills and procedures resulted directly from this disaster.
